commit.message:
Stop exempting .env.example from the private-key scan

check-secrets.sh folded two questions into one predicate: "may this file
be tracked?" and "may it contain a 64-hex literal?". Example env files
answer yes to the first, so they were also skipped for the second — which
inverts the check, because a file committed by definition is the likeliest
place for a real key to be pasted and published.

It was not hypothetical. extension/.env.example carried a live testnet key
inherited from upstream's fce-sign example, with 1319 transactions and a
balance on Coston2, and the scanner never mentioned it across five pushes.
No value was at risk — it is a shared example key on a testnet and this
project's own keys are generated into the gitignored .env — but a security
project should not publish a working key, and the scanner should not have
been the reason nobody noticed.

Splits the predicate in two, empties the key in the example file, and
verifies the scan now fails when a key is put back there.

Keep submission material out of the public repository

Removes the demo video project, the demo script and the submission notes
from tracking, and ignores them. They stay on disk; they are submission
artefacts rather than part of the product.

README no longer links to the two removed docs. The run instructions now
stand on preflight.sh alone, which is what they were pointing at anyway.

Add the demo video and the vision statement

A 3:10 scripted walkthrough, rendered with Remotion and narrated with
edge-tts. `npm run render` reproduces the submission file exactly — no
screen recording and no manual editing step to redo when a number
changes.

Two decisions worth recording.

The console shots are rebuilt rather than screen-recorded, with
src/theme.ts lifted verbatim from apps/web/app/globals.css. That keeps
the panels the product's own palette and type rather than a lookalike,
stays sharp at 1080p, and re-renders when the facts change.

Scene timing is derived from the audio instead of guessed.
generate-narration.py renders each block, measures it with ffprobe, and
writes real durations and caption cues; the composition keys scenes to
narration ids, so editing a line moves the visuals with it. The generator
refuses to write output when two blocks would overlap or the last runs
past the composition, and self-test.ts catches missing audio, orphaned
scenes and held frames before a multi-minute render rather than after.

Everything on screen is checkable: the deployed Coston2 addresses, and
the validated XRPL Testnet payment from the live ledger test, memo
included.

Also adds docs/vision.md for the DoraHacks submission field.

Deploy to Coston2 and bring the docs up to date

Both contracts are live and source-verified on Coston2:

  BridgeSafeController   0x32176FCA80690938194F30844501ea24Cf48b752
  BridgeSafeFdcVerifier  0x0B1B437183571ba99a5A27E1Ac980CA2ffd5b1D8

The verifier resolves its FDC anchor through Flare's ContractRegistry at
call time, confirmed live to return 0x906507E0B64bcD494Db73bd0459d1C667e14B933,
so the trust anchor cannot be repointed after deployment. Addresses are
recorded in docs/deployment.json by the deploy script.

Docs updated for the result relay, which was missing from the
architecture diagram and the demo script entirely — step 7 pointed at a
query-tee flag that does not exist, and nothing explained how a request
was supposed to leave CREATED. Adds the CHAIN and constructor-args
gotchas to the troubleshooting list, and corrects the test counts
(64 contracts, 34 extension, 14 services).

Rewrites the product framing to lead with what the system does and the
reasoning behind each boundary, rather than enumerating what it is not.
The security model stays stated in full — attestation mode is presented
as the deployment choice it is, since anyone who runs the stack sees it.

Fix two deployment blockers and pin the console ABI to the contract

Rehearsing scripts/deploy-coston2.sh against a fork of live Coston2
surfaced two defects that each stopped a first-time deployment dead.

.env set CHAIN=coston2. Foundry auto-loads .env for any forge or cast
command run from the repo root and reads $CHAIN as if it were --chain,
and its name for this network is flare-coston2 — so every such command
failed with "invalid value 'coston2' for '--chain'", including the manual
cast send steps in the demo script. Nothing in the repo read the
variable; the extension tooling sets its own. Removed, with a note in
.env.example explaining why the name is reserved, and an unset in the
deploy script in case a user's shell exports it.

--constructor-args is variadic, so the trailing --json was swallowed as
an extra constructor argument and forge refused to deploy. Moved last.

Separately: the console declares its own ABI fragments rather than
importing an artifact, which keeps the bundle small but leaves a seam
that fails in the worst way — change a struct in Solidity and the UI
still compiles, still type-checks, then throws the first time anyone
opens it, or renders confidently wrong values if a field is merely
reordered. CrossLanguage.t.sol pins this between Go and Solidity;
check-web-abi.ts is its TypeScript counterpart, and preflight runs it.

It caught the getTreasury change from the previous commit immediately.

Add result-relay: carry signed enclave decisions back to Flare

The contract dispatches an instruction and the enclave answers
asynchronously, leaving a signed result on the extension proxy. Nothing
collected it, so bindTreasuryAddress, submitAuthorization,
submitSignedPayment and confirmPolicy were never called by anything: a
treasury could not be bound, and every payment request stayed in CREATED
forever. broadcaster and fdc-worker sit downstream of results that never
arrived.

result-relay watches the four dispatching events, fetches each result
from the proxy, and delivers it to the matching controller method.

It looks powerful and is not. Every method it calls recovers the enclave
address from a signature over the result before changing state, so the
relay can only deliver a decision the enclave already made — it cannot
invent an authorization, alter an amount, or redirect a payment. Signed
refusals are delivered too, via submitFailure, so a declined request
fails cleanly and releases its reserved budget instead of sitting until
it expires. Anyone can run one; losing it delays payments rather than
stranding them.

The instruction id is read as the last non-indexed field of each event,
a convention the compiler cannot enforce — getting it wrong would stall
every payment with no error anywhere, so a test pins it, along with the
method signatures and the completeness of the routing table.

teeproxy restates the ActionResponse wire shape rather than importing
tee-node, keeping the services module's dependency tree small for the
same reason the ABI fragments are hand-written.

Guard confirmPolicy against replay of a superseded acknowledgement

An enclave ActionResult signature never expires, so every handler that
accepts one needs its own reason why the same bytes cannot be applied
twice. Payment requests have the state machine; bindTreasuryAddress has
the bound flag. A policy has no equivalent monotonic state, and
confirmPolicy had no guard at all.

Any address could therefore replay the enclave's acknowledgement of an
older policy and reinstate looser published spending limits. The
second-order effect was worse: the enclave declines any instruction whose
header commitment disagrees with its cached policy, so the rollback also
desynced the two and stopped the treasury paying entirely — repeatably,
for the cost of one transaction, with no way for the owner to stay ahead
of it.

requestPolicyUpdate now records the pending commitment and confirmPolicy
spends it, so an acknowledgement is valid exactly once and only for terms
the owner published on chain. It also means the enclave can no longer
install limits of its own choosing.

While here: refuse a cumulative cap below already-reserved spend, which
keeps reservedDrops <= maxTotalDrops true for the life of the treasury
and stops availableDrops underflowing.

The policy path had no functional tests, which is how this survived 58 of
them. Adds six, covering replay, an unrequested confirmation, double
confirmation, substituted terms, the happy path, and the reserved-spend
floor.

Submission docs, deploy script and licence

README, architecture, threat model and a demo script that takes a reviewer from
an empty machine to a settled payment. docs/submission.md answers every field on
the submission form, including an explicit split of what was written, what was
forked from fce-sign, and what was reused unchanged.

The threat model names, for each attack, which component has to misbehave and
which test covers it. Limitations are stated rather than glossed: simulated
attestation by default, privacy ends at settlement, single enclave, public
ciphertext, no audit, single-key governance. Traction is reported as none,
because there is none.

Also corrects three claims in SECURITY.md that had run ahead of the code. It
promised a dev-local.sh, a verify-images.sh and digest-pinned Flare images that
do not exist. Replaced with what is actually true: the offline path is the test
suites, Flare's images are referenced by tag as they publish them, and the
indexer is pinned by INDEXER_REF in infra/versions.env.

Console UI and the enclave payload builder

The console's centre of gravity is the execution trace: each step names what
vouches for it, so a judge can read one screen and see which stage the enclave
decided, which XRPL executed, and which the Data Connector proved. Settlement is
shown as an asynchronous stage with its real 90-180s latency rather than implied
to be instant.

payload-builder exists because the TEE node decrypts with go-ethereum's
crypto/ecies (ECIES_AES128_SHA256) while the common JavaScript ECIES libraries
use AES-256-GCM and a different KDF — a payload sealed in the browser would
decrypt to garbage inside the enclave. Keeping the scheme in Go guarantees the
match; a round-trip test decrypts through the same library the enclave uses, for
compressed, uncompressed and raw key encodings. It binds to loopback only and
refuses to start otherwise.

Upgraded next 15.5.4 -> 16.2.12 (CVE-2025-66478) and viem to clear its ws
advisory. The remaining audit finding is sharp, which Next pulls in for image
optimisation that this app never uses.

Relayer services and local infrastructure

broadcaster watches PaymentSigned, submits the blob the event carries, and
reports the transaction id back. fdc-worker watches PaymentBroadcast and runs
the Flare Data Connector round trip: prepare, submit to FdcHub, wait for round
finalisation, fetch the Merkle proof, hand it to the verifier contract.

Both are deliberately unprivileged. Their hand-written ABI fragments are the
whole of their on-chain reach: neither can create a treasury, open a request or
authorize a payment, and neither holds an XRPL key. Compromising them delays
payments rather than redirecting them.

infra/ runs our own C-chain indexer against public Coston2, which removes the
dependency on Flare handing out credentials to theirs. The ext-proxy cannot tell
the difference.

check-bindings.sh caught a real issue while being wired up: the upstream fce-sign
compose defaults the proxy to 0.0.0.0, publishing it to the whole local network.
Changed to 127.0.0.1 — the tunnel reaches loopback fine. The checker now resolves
${VAR:-default} so it judges what actually binds, verified in both directions.

FCC extension: in-enclave XRPL treasury signer

Forked from flare-foundation/fce-sign for its deploy and registration tooling,
then replaced the handlers with a treasury policy engine.

The XRPL codec is written from scratch rather than pulled in, and that is the
security property: it serializes exactly one shape, a native-XRP Payment with a
single memo. There is no field table, no transaction-type parameter and no
escape hatch, so nothing reachable from a decrypted instruction can turn a
payment into a TrustSet, an account rekey, or a token transfer.

Authorize and sign are separate commands. The signing step is told only which
request to sign; the terms come from enclave memory, so a payment cannot be
authorized on one set of terms and signed on another. One authorization yields
at most one signature.

Verified against the live ledger: TestLive_PaymentIsAcceptedByTheLedger funds a
generated address from the testnet faucet, submits a signed payment and gets
tesSUCCESS with the predicted transaction id and the memo intact. FDC then
reports that transaction with exactly the fields BridgeSafeFdcVerifier compares.

Also retunes the secret scanner. Flagging every 64-hex literal produced ~20
false positives per commit from keccak constants and test vectors, and a scanner
that cries wolf gets bypassed. It now requires the line to name a secret, except
inside .env files where nothing else belongs. Re-verified against five real leak
shapes.

58 contract tests (6 cross-language) and 26 Go tests.

Flare contracts: policy-controlled XRPL treasury with FDC-proven settlement

BridgeSafeController is both the treasury/request state machine and the FCC
InstructionSender, so every field it puts into an enclave instruction is
authenticated by construction. BridgeSafeFdcVerifier is deliberately separate:
it holds the eight conditions that let a request reach SETTLED, and nothing else.

Settlement requires an FDC XRPPayment proof matching source account, destination,
exact amount and a per-request memo reference, with each XRPL transaction id
consumable once. Policy limits are re-checked on chain, so a compromised enclave
still cannot exceed the published caps unnoticed.

52 tests: full lifecycle plus every negative case in the plan's phase 6.
